entries.test: Public evaluations of contemporary GPT chess play and controlled comparisons of correlational move generation with explicit board-and-rule tracking could test whether reliance on correlations causes recurring illegal moves.
entries.note: The surrounding paragraph grounds the general language about fragility in a concrete failure to follow chess rules.
There is no agreed set of GPT-5 “fantasies” or criterion for whether they “reckon with” the stated limitation. The embedded claim about inference capabilities could be tested separately.

entries.test: Public operational evaluations could establish whether military applications of the described correlational systems succeed or instead fail because they cannot reliably infer answers to novel questions.
entries.note: “Would be toast” expresses a firm predicted failure, with an explicit causal explanation. A demonstrated successful application would challenge the universal claim.

entries.test: Public technical disclosures and controlled factual-inference evaluations of LinkedIn’s assistant could test whether it represents Yurieff’s actual history and whether missing representations cause unreliable inferences about her.
entries.note: An internal computational representation is potentially inspectable technical evidence, unlike a private human intention. Lack of a guarantee does not mean every statement must be false.
Neither “pretending” nor getting “closer to safe AI” identifies an agreed intervention or outcome. The embedded word “might” is not a probability hedge on Marcus’s own assertion.
